title: Told incorrect information during sale of a contract
situation: I was told something untrue about what I was buying before I signed the contract.
points: For a contract to supply a service, anything said or written to the consumer, by or on behalf of the trader, about the trader or the service that the consumer took into account — when deciding to enter the contract, or in a later decision about the service — is treated as a term of the contract, subject to anything said on the same occasion that qualified it and any change expressly agreed.

A false statement that induced the contract may be a misrepresentation; the right to rescind on that ground is not lost merely because the statement became a term of the contract or the contract has been performed, subject to the other provisions of the Misrepresentation Act 1967.

Where the other party to a contract made a non-fraudulent misrepresentation that caused loss, damages may be recovered from them unless they prove they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe, it was true — but not where the consumer instead has a right to redress under the Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations 2008.
A fraudulent misrepresentation is actionable only where it induced the person to act to their detriment; it is not necessary to prove the person believed the statement was true.
A representation can be a continuing one, lasting until the contract is concluded; where it does, the person who made it may be taken to have assumed responsibility for its accuracy.

An unfair term of a consumer contract — one that, contrary to the requirement of good faith, causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations to the consumer's detriment — is not binding on the consumer.
